name: Esther Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential; could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther Khan, twenty-seven, and I run haulage equipment at a large copper mine. I check the machine and radio before the shift, then work the control station and coach operators when a load or route gets awkward. I like the focus of it, though the dust and twelve-hour roster can leave me wrung out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the job do you take most pride in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I can hear when a loader is straining before the screen shows a fault. I also stay calm on the radio, which matters when a new operator is backing near the crusher. My partner Daniel works as an electrician, and we have a good cushion but no children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a tool that saves ten minutes on a shift is still worth using, as long as the operator stays responsible. At the mine, I wouldn't want anyone calling a tidy screen a substitute for hearing the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job seems steady in this picture because the hard part is running equipment safely, not writing reports. I already use software every day, but I don't expect a small improvement to change my pay or standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my normal roster and keep showing the two newer operators how to read the machine's sound. I'd test any approved planning tool on a quiet shift, but I wouldn't spend our savings chasing a minor upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm; I have a solid trade and Daniel's income too. I do wonder whether the junior crew will get enough practice if a screen starts doing their checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine task would you hand to the software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let it sort maintenance notes by urgency, because that is dull desk work and easy to review. I would still walk around the loader before I signed it back into service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the crew how to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd show them the tool and make them explain its suggestion in their own words. A new operator needs to know when the machine's sound disagrees with a green box.

say: I'd welcome **small time savings** if the operator stays responsible for the machine.
I'd tell the crew that **a screen cannot hear** a loader struggling.
think: My **hands-on role** and pay look steady in this mild picture.
I worry that junior operators may lose **practice**, even if my own work barely shifts.
do: **Keep my** usual roster and coach two newer operators on machine sounds.
**Test an** approved maintenance tool on a quiet shift before recommending it.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own income, with a small concern about training.
S0.quote: A new operator needs to know when the machine's sound disagrees with a green box.
fieldNote: Esther ties competence to **listening**, not just reading a display.
Her steady income supports a calm response, while she notices the crew's lost practice time and the value of **hands-on coaching**.

steps.text: Keep the usual mine roster and coach two newer operators
Test the approved maintenance tool on a quiet shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine can use AI for shift notes and parts orders, but it should be clear who checks the result. I wouldn't call it a crisis while the machines still need people on the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The desk side of my team could get leaner before the loaders change. If fewer coordinators are needed, senior operators might inherit more planning, and I could be good at that but lose the part of the job I enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the mine's scheduling and diagnostics tools with our maintenance lead, not just click through a demo. In the first year I'd ask to shadow the control-room planner for a week and keep my equipment qualification current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see ways to stay useful. There are plenty of mines and contractors nearby, so I wouldn't assume one change means I have to leave the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if a coordinator you like was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rina, our shift coordinator, that I valued how she kept the crew from being sent to the wrong face. I'd help her check openings at the nearby sites, though I'd know that is easier said than done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you refuse a planning tool's recommendation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If its route sent a loaded vehicle across a zone with a weak radio signal, I'd stop and ask for a human review. The software doesn't stand beside the map when a crew is waiting.

say: I'd support **AI notes** if someone clearly checks the result.
I'd say the loaders still need **people at the controls** in this scenario.
think: My team could lose **coordination roles** before operators lose hands-on work.
I could learn planning, though I don't want to give up the **equipment** that I enjoy.
do: **Learn mine** scheduling and diagnostics with the maintenance lead.
**Shadow the** control-room planner for a week and renew my equipment qualification.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with nearby employers giving me room to adapt.
S1.quote: The software doesn't stand beside the map when a crew is waiting.
fieldNote: Esther accepts task automation but insists on **human review** for safety calls.
She links her own flexibility to learning planning while showing concern for **Rina**, the coordinator.

steps.text: Learn mine scheduling and diagnostics beside the maintenance lead
Keep my equipment qualification current while shadowing the planner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have two years before the thinking jobs change and about three more before robots can do the physical work. A mine should use that gap to train people instead of pretending the old roster will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and diagnosis parts of my job would be exposed right away, even if I still drive equipment until 2031. Once the robots arrive, I could lose the work I built my reputation on, and that would hit my income as well as my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask the mine for a written path into machine maintenance and keep putting money aside from each pay. In 2029 I'd apply for technician roles that involve inspecting and repairing equipment, knowing those roles could also change when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not helpless; we have savings and I can learn, but I can't assume a nearby job stays open. I'd have to make the move before the machines arrive, not wait for a layoff letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maintenance still be a secure career after the thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can't call it secure when the card says AI can do almost any thinking work. I mean the physical inspection may buy me some time, but by 2031 robots can do hands-on work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel I want us to keep our plans flexible instead of taking on a bigger mortgage this year. We could live on our current income while I try for a maintenance place, then decide again when we know what the mine is doing.

say: I'd say the mine has **two years to prepare** for thinking AI and about three more before hands-on robots.
I'd ask management to **train people early** instead of assuming today's roster lasts.
think: My planning work faces AGI first, and my operating work may end when **robots arrive in 2031**.
My savings help, but the change could cost my **income and pride**.
do: **Ask the** mine for a written route into machine maintenance and save more from each pay.
**Apply for** equipment technician roles in 2029, while accepting they may change too.
feel: I feel **anxious but capable** because the time window is short, though I have savings.
S2.quote: No, I can't call it secure when the card says AI can do almost any thinking work.
fieldNote: Esther explicitly corrects her first idea of maintenance as a **safe fallback**.
She uses her savings and nearby jobs as a bridge, while keeping the couple's **housing plans flexible**.

steps.text: Save more from each mine pay while requesting a maintenance path
Apply for equipment technician roles during 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready, not enough time to ignore it. At the mine, I'd want a real training schedule and honest dates for when the equipment fleet changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the next few years to move toward maintenance, but the thinking part of that work gets exposed in 2031 too. The physical repair side might last until 2034, yet I don't know whether a human technician will still be needed then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the technical college near town about its evening electrical maintenance course and enroll this winter if the hours fit my roster. In 2032, my first year after AGI, I'd look for a repair job while building a second option with Daniel's electrical business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but five years lets me make choices before a decision is made for me. I still wouldn't put all our savings into a course or a business that could be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the college teaches only screen-based diagnostics, I'd ask whether the qualification includes real equipment work before paying. I don't want to buy a certificate for tasks that AGI can already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel's business add to your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel knows the local wiring rules and has customers who need reliable repairs, while I know heavy equipment. We could test one small contract together, but I wouldn't treat it as a guaranteed living.

say: I'd say five years gives us **time to prepare**, and the mine should publish a real training schedule.
I'd ask for clear fleet-change dates so workers can **plan honestly**.
think: Maintenance offers a bridge, but its thinking tasks face **AGI in 2031** too.
A physical repair role may last to 2034, though I can't count on **lasting demand**.
do: **Enroll in** an evening electrical maintenance course this winter if it fits my roster.
**Look for** repair work in 2032 and test one small contract with Daniel.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with enough time to choose but no guaranteed safe job.
S3.quote: I don't want to buy a certificate for tasks that AGI can already do.
fieldNote: Esther wants training tied to **real equipment work**, not abstract credentials.
She treats Daniel's business as a trial option rather than assuming it can replace **her wage**.

steps.text: Enroll in an evening electrical maintenance course this winter if roster allows
Look for equipment repair work during 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a chance to prepare, but it isn't a promise that anyone's job will survive. People should keep learning while they still have choices and good pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At thirty-seven, I'd still be young enough to change direction, and I could use mine work to build savings while I do. My control work faces the robot date in 2039, so I can't treat the extra years as a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating and coaching through the years before 2036, while taking one accredited maintenance course at a time. In 2037 I'd move toward a hands-on equipment service role if a local employer still needs people, and I'd keep our savings diversified rather than buying a workshop on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the two-year picture because I can stage the change. I still feel a pinch thinking that robots could reach the repair work by 2039, but I don't need to rush into a bad bet today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Daniel change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about children on our own timetable, not bring them forward because of an AI date. If we decide to have a child, I'd want Daniel and me to choose it for the life we want, not as insurance against work changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your younger operators to remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that being excellent at one machine is valuable, but it shouldn't be the only thing on their work record. I learned early that a good crew trusts you because you notice the person beside you, not because your title is senior.

say: I'd call a decade a **chance to prepare**, not a guarantee that jobs survive.
I'd encourage workers to learn while they still have **good choices and pay**.
think: I could change direction at thirty-seven, and use my current wage to **build savings gradually**.
My hands-on work faces robots in 2039, so the extra years are only a **temporary bridge**.
do: **Keep operating** and coaching while taking accredited maintenance courses one at a time.
**Move toward** local equipment service work in 2037 if employers still need people.
feel: I feel **calmer with time**, though the later robot date still worries me.
S4.quote: I'd say a decade is a chance to prepare, but it isn't a promise that anyone's job will survive.
fieldNote: More warning gives Esther a **staged plan**, rather than certainty about an occupation.
She refuses to let a technology forecast dictate **family timing**, even as she plans a staged work transition.

steps.text: Keep operating and coaching until the 2036 thinking-AI date
Take accredited maintenance courses one at a time before 2036
Move toward local equipment service work in 2037 if available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking parts change quickly and the robots follow before I can settle into a new trade. A paid transition course and clear notice from the mine would help me plan without draining our savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd ask whether the people who know the machines get a say before a site replaces them. A safe shift depends on what operators notice, and that knowledge should count even when the screen can do more of the paperwork.

headlineQuote: A safe shift depends on what operators notice, and that knowledge should count even when the screen can do more of the paperwork.
portrait: Esther Khan is **twenty-seven**, a senior mine equipment operator with a technical diploma and a strong savings cushion.
She is **adaptable and curious**, yet believes safe work still needs people who know the machines.
She stays **calm in mild change**, but sees income risk when thinking AI and later robots reach her work.
She uses extra warning to retrain in stages and keeps her **family decisions personal**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries me because thinking work changes quickly and robots follow before I can settle into another trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid transition course** and clear notice from the mine would let me plan without draining our savings.
